title: Rocks and Landscapes
description: Ten short stories about the ground beneath our feet: how mountains rise and wear down, a road cut, a cave, the ice that made the Great Lakes, the volcanoes of the Cascades, a rock shop, earthquakes, a granite quarry, a river stone and a miner's granddaughter.
topic: Geology, rocks and the shape of the land

lessons.title: How Mountains Rise and Wear Down
lessons.summary: On a hike in the Appalachians, a retired science teacher explains to her grandson how mountains are pushed up and slowly worn away.
lessons.text:
Ellen, a retired science teacher, liked nothing better than a long walk in the mountains with her grandson, Leo. Leo was twelve and inclined to ask questions about everything.

One morning in October, they climbed a ridge in the Appalachians. The trail was steep and rocky, and halfway up, Leo sat down on a log. "These mountains are too big," he said. "Not at all," said Ellen. "These are some of the oldest mountains in the world, and they are only a shadow of what they once were. They may once have been as high as the Himalayas."

A squirrel ran along a branch above his head. "Then where did the rest of the mountains go?" he asked.

"First you have to know how mountains rise," Ellen said. "The outer shell of the earth is broken into huge plates, which move about as fast as your nails grow. About three hundred million years ago, two plates pushed together here, and the rock between them had nowhere to go. It was pushed upward. Layers that had lain flat on the bottom of a sea were bent and warped like a rug pushed against a wall."

She pointed to a rock beside the trail with gray and white stripes curved like a wave. "You can still see warped layers like these. They are not uncommon here."

"Then why aren't the mountains still high?"

"Because the moment a mountain begins to rise, it also begins to wear down. Rain washes away grains of sand. In winter, water gets into small cracks, freezes and pushes the cracks wider, so pieces break off. Rivers carry the pieces to the sea. Each year the change is tiny, but over two hundred million years, tiny changes add up to whole mountains."

Leo wanted to know who had figured that out.

"One of the first people to understand this was a Scot named James Hutton, who lived more than two hundred years ago. He studied the rocks of his country extensively, and he saw that slow forces like rain and frost could shape the land if the earth was very old. In his time, that idea was problematic, because most people believed the earth was only a few thousand years old. But the Scot traveled extensively and collected evidence, and in the end, the evidence was on his side."

"And the plates?"

"That idea came only about sixty years ago. It unified many old puzzles: why the coasts of Africa and South America fit together, why earthquakes come in long lines, and why the highest mountains stand where plates meet. The puzzles formed one unified picture. Such moments are not uncommon in science."

At the top, they ate their sandwiches while the squirrel watched, hoping for bread. "So we are sitting on what is left of a much taller mountain," he said.

"Exactly," said Ellen, and she was inclined to think that he would remember it.

Questions:
Why did Leo sit down halfway up the trail?
He thought the mountains were too big.
How do mountains rise, according to Ellen?
When two plates push together, the rock between them is warped and pushed upward.
How does frost help to wear mountains down?
Water gets into small cracks, freezes and pushes the cracks wider, so pieces of rock break off.
Why was James Hutton's idea problematic in his time?
Most people believed the earth was only a few thousand years old.
What did the idea of moving plates do?
It unified many old puzzles into one picture.

lessons.title: Reading a Road Cut
lessons.summary: A scientist who studies rocks stops at a highway road cut with his niece and shows her how to read its layers from the bottom up.
lessons.text:
Nina was seventeen, and in the spring she would be a contestant in the state science competition, in an event about rocks and minerals. Her uncle Marcus, who studied rocks for the state, had promised to help her prepare. One morning, he picked her up in his old truck and drove west.

After an hour, he steered the truck onto a wide shoulder. On both sides of the road rose a high wall of rock, where engineers had blasted a path through a ridge.

"This is a road cut," Marcus said. "When engineers build a highway through a hill, they cut straight through it. The specs for the road tell them how steep the walls can be, so that rocks don't fall onto the cars. For the engineers, it's just a wall that meets the specs. For us, it's a book with every page open."

Nina looked at the cut. Most drivers who passed it were completely unaware that they were driving past a history of the land. She had been unaware of it too, until that moment.

"The trick is to be systematic," Marcus said. "Layers of rock are laid down one on top of another, so the oldest is usually at the bottom. We start at the bottom and work up."

At the base of the cut was a thick layer of gray limestone. Nina looked closely and saw tiny shells in it. "This was the floor of a warm, shallow sea," Marcus said. "Those animals lived and died there, and their shells became part of the rock."

Above the limestone lay a layer of red sandstone. "Sand like this collects near a coast or in a river," he explained. "So the sea became shallower, and the shore moved closer." Higher still was a thin black stripe. "Coal," he said. "That was a swamp full of plants. Slowly, the plants turned into coal."

Then the sun came out from behind a cloud and began to illuminate the whole wall. Now Nina noticed something she had missed. The layers were not flat. They curved down in the middle, like a giant bowl.

"Good," said Marcus. "Long after the layers formed, two plates pushed against each other and bent them. The light illuminates the shape beautifully, doesn't it?"

Nina drew the layers in her notebook in order, from the bottom to the top. "That's exactly how a contestant should work," he said. "Be systematic, describe what you see and only then explain it."

As Marcus steered back onto the highway, Nina asked him what she should study at college. She was a prospective student at three universities, and one of them had an excellent earth science program. "Visit them all," Marcus said, "but as a prospective scientist, you already have the most important skill. You know how to look, and at seventeen, that's rare."

Questions:
Why did Marcus take Nina to the road cut?
He wanted to help her prepare for the state science competition.
What do the specs for a road tell the engineers?
They tell the engineers how steep the walls can be.
Why should you read a road cut from the bottom up?
Layers are laid down one on top of another, so the oldest is usually at the bottom.
What did Nina notice when the sun began to illuminate the wall?
She noticed that the layers curved down like a giant bowl.
What skill did Marcus say Nina already had?
He said she already knew how to look.

lessons.title: How a Cave Is Made
lessons.summary: A cave guide in Kentucky explains how water carves a cave out of rock and then decorates it, and an old visitor remembers his first trip there.
lessons.text:
Maria had worked as a guide at a large cave in Kentucky for eleven summers, and she still began every tour in the same place: at the wide, dark mouth of the cave, where cool air flowed out to meet the warm afternoon.

"This entrance is a gateway," she told the group. "Through this gateway, you are about to walk into a world that water has been making for more than a million years."

In the group that day was an old man named Walter, who walked with a cane. He told Maria that he had first visited the cave as a boy of nine. "That trip kindled my love of rocks," he said, tapping the floor with his cane. "Seventy years later, the fire is still burning." Maria smiled. Nothing pleased her more than hearing that a visit had kindled an interest for life.

Inside, she stopped beside a gray wall. "This is limestone," she said. "Rain picks up a gas called carbon dioxide from the air and the soil, which turns the water into a very weak acid. For thousands of years, that acid water ran through small cracks in the limestone, and grain by grain, it dissolved the rock. The cracks grew into tunnels, and the tunnels grew into rooms like this one."

"Is it still happening?" a girl asked.

"Yes. Far below us, an underground river is still at work. The process is underway right now, though it is far too slow to see." Maria liked that idea: the making of the cave was still underway.

Then Maria lifted her light toward the ceiling, where hundreds of stone icicles hung down, and others rose from the floor to meet them. "Here is the great irony of caves," she said. "The same water that dissolved the rock now builds these shapes. When a drop of water reaches the air in the cave, some of the gas escapes, and the drop leaves a tiny bit of rock behind. Drop by drop, the cave is decorated by the water that made it."

She told them that the early settlers had thought the cave was haunted, because of the strange echoes and the sound of water in the dark. "It isn't haunted," she said, "but I understand why they thought so."

Then her voice became more serious. "Years ago, some visitors illegally broke off pieces of these shapes to take home. A piece that took ten thousand years to grow can be destroyed in a second." Every year, she added, a few pieces came back in the mail, with letters asking for forgiveness. "We forgive them," she said, "but we can never put the pieces back."

When the group came out, the sun was setting. Soon bats began to pour from the entrance like a flock of birds. Walter watched the flock disappear over the trees and said quietly, "Some things haven't changed at all."

Questions:
Why did Maria call the entrance a gateway?
Through it, visitors enter a world made by water.
How did water make the cave?
A very weak acid in the water ran through cracks in the limestone and dissolved the rock.
What is the great irony of caves, according to Maria?
The same water that dissolved the rock now decorates the cave.
Why did the early settlers think the cave was haunted?
They heard strange echoes and the sound of water in the dark.
What do some letters in the mail ask for?
They ask for forgiveness for pieces that were broken off illegally.

lessons.title: What the Ice Left Behind
lessons.summary: On a trip from Lake Michigan to Niagara Falls, a mother tells her son how great sheets of ice shaped the Great Lakes.
lessons.text:
One summer, Karen took her son, Ben, on a long drive around the Great Lakes, from the shore of Lake Michigan to Niagara Falls. Ben was ten, and Karen wanted him to understand how the lakes had been made.

On the first evening, they sat on the beach. "Twenty thousand years ago," Karen said, "this whole place was under ice. A sheet of ice up to two miles thick covered Canada and the north of this country. It weighed many trillions of tons."

"How much is a trillion?" Ben asked.

"A million millions," she said. "The ice was so heavy that it pressed the land down. The ground beneath it had to flex, the way a bed flexes when you lie on it. Now that the ice is gone, the land in the north is still slowly rising, like a bed that flexes back when you get up."

The next day, they drove past fields full of large stones. Many of them were a different kind of rock from the ground beneath them. "The ice carried those stones from far to the north," Karen explained. "When it melted, it had to discard everything it was carrying. So it discarded stones from Canada in the middle of farms in Ohio."

The lakes, she told him, had begun as river valleys. The ice followed the valleys and scraped them deeper, until they became huge basins. When the ice melted, water filled the basins. The first lakes were larger than today's and kept changing shape as the ice pulled back. "Today's lakes are their descendants," she said. "Every lake you see is a descendant of the meltwater."

In the afternoon, they stopped near a long, low ridge made of sand and stones. "The ice pushed this up at its edge," Karen said. "Ridges like this partition the land the way walls partition a house into rooms, and many of those rooms are full of ponds and wet ground." Ben slapped his arm. "And full of mosquitoes," he said. The mosquitoes were the price of all that water.

That water was the real gift of the ice. The Great Lakes hold about one fifth of all the fresh water on the surface of the earth. "Few places have such an abundance of fresh water," Karen said. "People forget what an abundance it is, until there is a dry summer somewhere else."

On the last day, they stood at Niagara Falls. The water from Lake Erie rushed toward the edge and seemed to pause for a moment before it began to plunge over the cliff, on its way to Lake Ontario. "When the ice left, this river was born," Karen said. "For twelve thousand years, the water has been eating the cliff away, so the falls have moved back about seven miles." Ben watched the water plunge into the white cloud below. He did not say anything for a long time.

Questions:
How heavy was the sheet of ice?
It weighed many trillions of tons.
Why is the land in the north still slowly rising?
The ice pressed the land down, and now that the ice is gone, the ground is flexing back.
Why are there stones from Canada on farms in Ohio?
The ice carried them south and discarded them when it melted.
Why did Karen call today's lakes descendants?
They are descendants of the larger lakes formed by the melting ice.
What does the water do at Niagara Falls?
It plunges over a cliff on its way to Lake Ontario.

lessons.title: A Trilogy of Volcanoes
lessons.summary: A filmmaker finishing a trilogy about the volcanoes of the Cascades talks to a scientist about Mount St. Helens and about what the future may bring.
lessons.text:
Jonah was a filmmaker from Portland, and for five years he had been working on a trilogy of films about the volcanoes of the Cascades, the chain of mountains that runs from northern California into Canada. The first film of the trilogy explained how the volcanoes form. The second told the story of Mount St. Helens. The third, which he was finishing now, asked what might happen next.

For the last film, he interviewed Dr. Grace Lin, a scientist who had watched the Cascades for most of her life.

"Why are there volcanoes here at all?" Jonah asked.

"Off the coast, a plate of the ocean floor is sliding slowly under the edge of this continent," Grace said. "As it sinks deep into the earth, it heats up and releases water. That water helps the hot rock above it melt. The melted rock is lighter than the rock around it, so it rises, and where it reaches the surface, a volcano grows."

"Tell me about the spring of 1980."

"In March, small earthquakes began under the mountain. Then the activity began to escalate: more earthquakes, then steam explosions. By April, the north side of the mountain was swelling outward by about five feet a day. Everyone could see that it was unstable. On the morning of May 18, an earthquake shook the unstable side loose, and it slid away in the largest landslide ever recorded. Without that weight, the gas inside the mountain burst out sideways."

"And the forests?"

"The blast shredded forests across more than two hundred square miles. Huge trees were snapped like matches. Some areas looked as if a giant had shredded them with his hands. The mountain lost more than a thousand feet of its height."

Jonah showed her an old photograph of the gray, empty hills after the blast, and then a new one of the same slopes, green with young trees. "Your next subject is renewal," he said.

"Yes, and renewal came faster than anyone expected," Grace said. "Small animals had survived underground. Flowers grew in the ash. Within a few years, elk returned. Watching that renewal has been one of the joys of my life."

"Are you optimistic about the future?"

"About warnings, I am optimistic. In 1980 we had a few instruments. Today, hundreds of instruments sit on these mountains, and their readings are transmitted to us every second. When a mountain begins to wake up, those transmitted signals can give us weeks or months of warning."

When the trilogy was finished, Jonah's studio designed the promotional poster: three mountains in a row under a red sky. Grace saw the promotional poster in a theater in Seattle and laughed. "Very dramatic," she wrote to the filmmaker. "The real mountains are calmer than that, most days."

Questions:
What was each part of Jonah's trilogy about?
The first explained how the volcanoes form, the second told the story of Mount St. Helens, and the third asked about the future.
Why do volcanoes form in the Cascades?
A plate of the ocean floor sinks under the continent and releases water, which helps the rock above it melt.
How did the activity at Mount St. Helens escalate in 1980?
First there were small earthquakes, then steam explosions, and then the north side began to swell.
What did the blast do to the forests?
It shredded forests across more than two hundred square miles.
Why is Grace optimistic about warnings?
Readings from hundreds of instruments are transmitted every second and can give weeks or months of warning.

lessons.title: The Rock Shop on Main Street
lessons.summary: The owner of a small rock shop shows a boy and his mother around her trays of stones, a salt crystal, a meteorite and a piece of amber.
lessons.text:
Gloria had owned the rock shop on Main Street for twenty-two years. It was a narrow room full of glass cases and wooden shelves, and near the door stood a long table covered with trays of polished stones. When Gloria was a girl, stones like these had cost a nickel each. Now they cost a dollar, but children still came in with coins in their hands and spent half an hour choosing.

One quiet afternoon, a boy named Owen came in with his mother. "There's an epidemic at his school," his mother said. "An epidemic of rock collecting. Half the class is bringing stones to show the teacher." Gloria smiled. It was her favorite kind of epidemic.

Owen went straight to the trays. In one tray were green and blue stones, in another, stones with bands of red and white. In the last tray, three kittens were asleep on a soft cloth. "They belong to the shop cat," Gloria said. "That tray is not for sale, but you can pet the kittens." Owen touched one kitten very gently, and it opened one eye.

Then she showed him a clear, square crystal. "This is salt," she said. "It's made of two elements, sodium and chlorine. The sodium in this crystal is the same sodium that's in the salt on your table."

"Is it tasty?" Owen asked.

"Salt makes food tasty," Gloria said, "but please don't lick my crystals. Plenty of customers have already tried."

In a glass case was a heavy, dark piece of metal. "This fell from the sky," she said. "It's a meteorite. It's mostly iron, with some nickel. Iron and nickel together are a sign that it came from deep inside a small planet that broke apart long ago."

Next to it was a piece of golden amber. Inside it, perfectly kept, was a mosquito. "Amber isn't really a rock," Gloria explained. "It's the hardened sap of an ancient tree. This mosquito landed on the sap and was trapped. The amber has kept it imprisoned for about forty million years." Owen stared at the tiny insect. It was hard to imagine anything imprisoned for so long.

Gloria also showed them her annex, a small room at the back where she cut and polished stones and made silver bracelets. The annex smelled of wet stone. She sold the bracelets in the shop and in an online marketplace, where people from all over the country could buy them. "The online marketplace keeps the shop alive," she said. "And a new tariff on stones from abroad has made local stones more popular. Because of the tariff, my prices look very fair."

Owen chose four stones from the trays and a small bracelet for his mother. At the door, he asked whether he could come back to see the kittens. "Of course," Gloria said. "And bring your friends from the epidemic."

Questions:
What was in the last tray on the table?
Three kittens that belonged to the shop cat were asleep in it.
What is salt made of?
It is made of sodium and chlorine.
What does the iron and nickel in the meteorite show?
They show that it came from deep inside a small planet that broke apart long ago.
How long has the amber kept the mosquito imprisoned?
It has kept the mosquito imprisoned for about forty million years.
Where does Gloria sell her bracelets?
She sells them in the shop and in an online marketplace.

lessons.title: Why the Ground Shakes
lessons.summary: A science teacher in San Francisco explains to her class why earthquakes happen and then leads an earthquake drill.
lessons.text:
Every fall, Ms. Ortiz taught her eighth-grade class about earthquakes. Her school was in San Francisco, so the subject was not just science.

She began the lesson in her classroom upstairs. "The outer shell of the earth is made of plates," she said. "Here in California, two of them meet. The Pacific plate is moving northwest, past the rest of the continent, about two inches a year. But the plates don't slide easily. They stick. The rock along the edge bends a little more every year, like a stick you are slowly bending in your hands."

She took a thin stick from her desk and bent it until it broke with a loud crack. Everyone jumped. "When the rock finally breaks and slips, all that stored energy is released at once. It travels through the ground as waves, and when those waves reach us, the ground shakes."

Then she told them about 1906. A great earthquake broke the ground for nearly three hundred miles. In the city, it broke the water pipes, the main arteries that carried water under the streets. Fires started, and with the arteries broken, there was little water to fight them. The fires burned for three days. "The earthquake did not destroy the city by itself," she said, "but it crippled the city's ability to save itself. A city whose arteries are cut is like a body that has lost its blood."

"Could that happen again?" asked a boy named Daniel.

"A big earthquake will happen again. But a crippled city is not something we have to accept. Today, tall buildings are designed to sway instead of breaking, the way a tree sways in the wind. Old brick buildings that could fall were judged an unacceptable risk, and many of them have been made stronger."

Next, the class used a shake table, a flat board on a motor, to simulate an earthquake. The students put their paper towers on it, and the table began to simulate stronger and stronger shaking. The stiff towers fell. The ones that could sway stood longest.

"Now, what about your home?" she asked. "Heavy appliances can move or fall. Ask your parents to fix tall shelves and appliances to the wall. Our school did the same thing: the old boiler in the basement used to stand loose, which was unacceptable. Last summer, the boiler was bolted to the floor."

At the end of the lesson, an alarm rang for the drill. Every student dropped to the floor and squatted under a desk, holding on to its leg. "Squat low and cover your head," Ms. Ortiz called. After a minute, they left the classroom upstairs and went out to the playground, far from the walls of the building. On the playground, she counted every student. All twenty-eight were there.

"Good," she said. "Now you know what to do."

Questions:
Why does the ground shake in an earthquake?
The rock along the edge of a plate bends until it breaks and slips, and the energy travels as waves.
How did the earthquake of 1906 cripple the city?
It broke the main water arteries, so there was little water to fight the fires.
Why are tall buildings designed to sway?
A building that can sway does not break as easily.
What did the class use to simulate an earthquake?
They used a shake table, a flat board on a motor.
What did the students do during the drill?
They squatted under their desks and then went out to the playground.

lessons.title: The Quarry Vote
lessons.summary: A reporter in a small granite town describes a calm election in which the main question is whether the old quarry should open again.
lessons.text:
I have written for the weekly newspaper in our small town in Vermont for fifteen years, and I have never seen an election so focused on a single hole in the ground.

The hole is the old quarry on the hill. For more than a century, our town cut granite from it. Granite forms deep underground, when melted rock cools so slowly that large crystals have time to grow. That is why you can see the grains in it: white, gray and black, like salt and pepper. Our granite is hard and fine, and it stands in monuments across the country. The quarry closed thirty years ago, and this spring a company asked permission to open it again.

The incumbent mayor, Helen Ward, had held the office for eight years. She supported the plan, with strict conditions. Her opponent, a teacher named Paul Grady, said the conditions were not strong enough. The incumbent's slogan was "Our Stone, Our Jobs." Paul's slogan was "Protect the Hill." Both slogans were on signs all over town.

At a meeting in the school gym, both sides were polite, but the room was full of feeling. A group of high school students began a chant: "Protect the hill! Protect the hill!" The chant went on until Helen smiled and raised her hand. Later, a local comedian performed a parody that mixed both slogans, "Our Hill, Our Snacks," which made the whole room laugh. A good parody, I have learned, can calm a room faster than any speech.

The incumbent received an important endorsement from the stone carvers, many of whose grandfathers worked in the quarry. They endorsed her in a short letter that said the town had been built on granite and should not forget it. Paul was endorsed by a group of families who lived near the quarry road.

The most talked-about paper of the campaign was a memo from one of the mayor's aides. It listed every condition the company would have to meet, such as no blasting at night and trucks only on the main road. The aide shared the memo with our newspaper, and I printed it in full.

Some of those conditions have a history. Twenty years ago, a farmer named Roy Kessler was the plaintiff in a case against a company whose dust covered his fields. The plaintiff won, and the town wrote new rules because of his case.

We received more letters this spring than ever and printed nearly all of them, except for a few that were abusive. Our rule is simple: we print strong opinions, but never abusive ones.

In the end, Helen Ward won by two hundred votes, and the quarry will open next year under the conditions in the memo. Paul Grady called her the same evening to wish her well. On my way home, I passed a sign that still said "Protect the Hill," and I thought that, with such strict rules, both sides had won something.

Questions:
How does granite form?
It forms deep underground, when melted rock cools so slowly that large crystals have time to grow.
What were the two slogans in the election?
The incumbent's slogan was "Our Stone, Our Jobs," and Paul's was "Protect the Hill."
Who gave the incumbent an important endorsement?
The stone carvers endorsed her.
What was in the memo that the mayor's aide wrote?
It listed every condition the company would have to meet.
Why does the newspaper refuse to print some letters?
It never prints letters that are abusive.

lessons.title: The Story of a River Stone
lessons.summary: A nurse tells the long story of the smooth gray stone she keeps on her desk, from its birth deep underground to the river where she found it.
lessons.text:
I work as a nurse in a psychiatric hospital, and on my desk there is a smooth gray stone about the size of an egg. Patients often pick it up while we talk. Some of them come to us in deep despair, and I have noticed that holding something heavy and calm can help a person breathe more slowly. In psychiatric care, small things like that matter. Sometimes, when a patient asks about the stone, I tell its story.

I found the stone when I was eleven, on my uncle's ranch in Montana. My uncle trained horses, and every summer he worked with a bronco, a wild young horse that had never carried a rider. While he worked with the bronco in the field, I walked down to the river and looked at stones. That is where I found this one. Years later, a friend who studies rocks read its story for me.

The stone is granite. It was born deep underground, when a great mass of melted rock cooled over thousands of years and its crystals slowly grew. For millions of years it stayed there, buried under miles of other rock. Then the land above it was pushed up into mountains, and rain, ice and rivers wore away the rock on top, until the granite reached the surface.

Then the weather went to work. Winter storms would lash the mountain with rain and snow. Water ran into the cracks, froze and pushed them wider. One spring, after a winter of storms that lashed the high slopes for weeks, a block of granite broke away and fell into a stream.

That block broke into smaller pieces, and the stream began to carry them. In spring, when the snow melted, the water was fast and strong, and the stones rolled and knocked against each other. Every knock took off a tiny bit of a corner. In late summer, the water was slow, and the stones rested in slack water on the inside of the river's bends. In slack water, a stone could rest for years, until the next great flood moved it again.

After a long journey, our stone came to the ranch, smooth and rounded, its corners gone. That is where an eleven-year-old girl found it and carried it home in her pocket.

I clean it with a soft rag once a week. When I wipe it with the rag, the black and white grains shine. I like to tell my patients that this stone was broken, rolled and knocked about for a very long time, and that it became smoother, not weaker. I do not want to make anyone's pain seem small. But I have seen that story kindle a little hope in people who had none.

My uncle's bronco became the best horse on the ranch. Patience, it seems, works on horses and stones alike.

Questions:
Why do patients pick up the stone?
Holding something heavy and calm can help a person breathe more slowly, especially in despair.
Where did the writer find the stone?
She found it by the river on her uncle's ranch in Montana.
How did the block of granite break away from the mountain?
Storms lashed the mountain, and water froze in its cracks until the block broke away.
Where did the stones rest in late summer?
They rested in slack water on the inside of the river's bends.
How does the writer clean the stone?
She wipes it with a soft rag once a week.

lessons.title: The First in the Family
lessons.summary: A young woman graduates from a mining school with a degree in earth science, and her grandfather, a retired copper miner, comes to watch.
lessons.text:
On a bright morning in May, Anna Novak put on a black gown and a square black hat. In two hours, she would graduate from the state school of mines with a degree in earth science. She was the first person in her family to finish college, and everyone knew it was a milestone.

Her grandfather, Joe, had driven three hundred miles to be there. He was eighty-one and walked slowly, leaning on his cane. For forty years, he had worked underground in the copper mines of Butte, Montana. Joe was her mother's father. Her mother's maiden name was Kovac, one of the oldest mining names in Butte, and Anna was proud to carry that maiden name as her middle name.

Joe had left school at fifteen to work in the mines. All his life, he said, the lack of a diploma was a handicap. It kept him from better jobs, and it made him shy in front of educated people. But he never let that handicap stop him from learning. He read everything he could find about rocks and minerals, and he knew more about copper than many of Anna's teachers.

During her four years at the school, Anna and her grandfather had kept up a long correspondence. He wrote her a letter every week, and she wrote back. Their correspondence filled a box under her bed. In his letters, Joe often wrote about the brotherhood of the mines. Underground, he said, every man depended on the others for his life. That brotherhood, he wrote, was the thing he missed most.

At the ceremony, the president of the school asked the graduates to stand in their black gowns and turn toward their families. "Salute the people who brought you here," he said. Anna turned and found her grandfather in the crowd. He slowly raised his hand to his forehead in the old miners' salute that he had shown her as a child. She returned the salute, and she saw that his eyes were wet.

Afterward, the family had an informal party in the backyard of the house Anna had rented with two friends. It was very informal, with sandwiches and folding chairs on the grass. Anna stood up and thanked her grandfather. "Your letters taught me as much as my classes," she said. Her words were simple and sincere, and Joe nodded.

Then Joe stood up, leaning on his cane. "I spent forty years under the ground, in the dark," he said. "Now my granddaughter will study the ground in the daylight. That is the best thing a miner could ask for." It was a short speech, but it was the most sincere one Anna had ever heard. She put his words in the box with the rest of their correspondence.

Questions:
Why was Anna's graduation a milestone?
She was the first person in her family to finish college.
Why did Joe say the lack of a diploma was a handicap?
It kept him from better jobs and made him shy in front of educated people.
How did Anna and her grandfather keep in touch during her studies?
They kept up a long correspondence, writing letters every week.
What did Joe miss most about the mines?
He missed the brotherhood, because underground every man depended on the others.
What did Joe do when the graduates turned to salute their families?
He raised his hand to his forehead in the old miners' salute.
